blockMcqs.question: You must list every prime up to 10 million. Which tool?
blockMcqs.explanation: One sieve pass marks all primes up to N, then answers each query instantly.

blockMcqs.question: What is the time complexity of the Euclidean gcd algorithm?
blockMcqs.explanation: The remainder shrinks exponentially, so the count of steps is logarithmic.

blockMcqs.question: Why does the sieve start crossing out at p² rather than 2p?
options: p² is the first prime multiple of p
Smaller multiples were crossed by smaller primes
blockMcqs.explanation: Multiples like 2p or 3p already got marked when 2 and 3 were processed.

blockMcqs.question: Which operation does NOT distribute over a modulus?
blockMcqs.explanation: Division needs the modular inverse; the other three can be reduced at each step.

blockMcqs.question: Why is 1e9+7 chosen as the modulus, not a random round number?
options: It is prime and products stay within 64 bits
It is a power of two for fast masking
It guarantees no collisions in hashing
blockMcqs.explanation: Primality enables Fermat inverse; its size keeps any product under ~10¹⁸.

blockMcqs.question: In binary exponentiation, when is the base multiplied into the result?
options: Only when the current low bit of n is 1
Whenever the base exceeds the modulus
blockMcqs.explanation: Only set bits of the exponent contribute their squared power to the product.

blockMcqs.question: Fermat gives the modular inverse of a as which value?
blockMcqs.explanation: Raising a to m−2 yields x with a·x ≡ 1, valid when m is prime.

blockMcqs.question: When N ≈ 10¹², why avoid the sieve for primality?
options: It needs O(N) memory you can't allocate
It only works for prime N
blockMcqs.explanation: A trillion-entry boolean array is infeasible; trial-divide single numbers instead.

blockMcqs.question: Why prefer Pascal's triangle over factorials for small-N combinations?
options: It runs in O(1) per query
It avoids division and modular inverse
It uses less memory than factorials
It works without a prime modulus only
blockMcqs.explanation: Each cell is one addition, so there is no division bug to introduce.

blockMcqs.question: Why compute lcm as a / gcd(a,b) * b instead of a * b / gcd(a,b)?
options: The two formulas give different results
Dividing first avoids overflow on the product
gcd is undefined for the second form
blockMcqs.explanation: a*b can exceed the integer max; dividing first keeps the intermediate small.
